claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The GLABRA2 transcription factor negatively regulates RSL class I genes in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana.
claims.source: The GLABRA2 transcription factor negatively regulates these genes in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on GLABRA2 function.

claims.claim: A mutant screen in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha identified FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1) microRNA (miRNA) that negatively regulates the RSL class I gene MpRSL1.
claims.source: To find negative regulators of RSL class I genes in early diverging land plants we conducted a mutant screen in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha. This identified FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1) microRNA (miRNA) that negatively regulates the RSL class I gene MpRSL1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutant screen described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The MpFRH1 miRNA and its mRNA target constitute a feedback mechanism that controls epidermal cell differentiation.
claims.source: The miRNA and its mRNA target constitute a feedback mechanism that controls epidermal cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mutual regulation between MpFRH1 and MpRSL1.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 miRNA target sites are conserved among liverwort RSL class I mRNAs but are not present in RSL class I mRNAs of other land plants.
claims.source: MpFRH1 miRNA target sites are conserved among liverwort RSL class I mRNAs but are not present in RSL class I mRNAs of other land plants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: While RSL class I genes are ancient and conserved, independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution.
claims.source: These findings indicate that while RSL class I genes are ancient and conserved, independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparative data showing different negative regulators in different lineages.

claims.claim: The rooting structures of the first land plants are likely to have comprised systems of tip-growing filamentous cells called rhizoids that are morphologically similar to root hairs of vascular plants.
claims.source: The rooting structures of the first land plants are likely to have comprised systems of tip-growing filamentous cells called rhizoids that are morphologically similar to root hairs of vascular plants (Edwards et al., 1995; Wellman et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2005; Kerp et al., 2003; Taylor, 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior paleobotanical research.

claims.claim: RSL class I genes promote root hair differentiation in the vascular plants rice (Oryza sativa), Brachypodium distachyon and Arabidopsis thaliana.
claims.source: RSL class I genes promote root hair differentiation in the vascular plants rice (Oryza sativa), Brachypodium distachyon and Arabidopsis thaliana (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Menand et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I genes in these species.

claims.claim: RSL class I genes positively regulate rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and rhizoid development in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha and the moss Physcomitrella patens.
claims.source: Similarly, RSL class I genes positively regulate rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and rhizoid development in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha and the moss Physcomitrella patens (Proust et al., 2016; Menand et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I genes in bryophytes.

claims.claim: Root hairs and rhizoids initiate from those epidermal cells that express RSL class I genes.
claims.source: Root hairs and rhizoids initiate from those epidermal cells that express RSL class I genes (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Menand et al., 2007; Jang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: Constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes is sufficient to modulate root hair patterning by inducing root hair development from any root epidermal cell in the monocots O. sativa and B. distachyon.
claims.source: Furthermore, constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes is sufficient to modulate root hair patterning by inducing root hair development from any root epidermal cell in the monocots O. sativa and B. distachyon (Zalewski et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I gene overexpression.

claims.claim: Constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes in the liverwort M. polymorpha and moss P. patens is sufficient to induce rhizoid formation from almost any epidermal cell of the gametophyte.
claims.source: Similarly, constitutive over-expression of RSL class I genes in the liverwort M. polymorpha and moss P. patens is sufficient to induce rhizoid formation from almost any epidermal cell of the gametophyte (Proust et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on RSL class I gene overexpression in bryophytes.

claims.claim: RSL class I genes function as molecular switches that are both necessary and sufficient to induce the root hair cell and rhizoid cell developmental program in epidermal cells.
claims.source: These findings indicate that RSL class I genes function as molecular switches that are both necessary and sufficient to induce the root hair cell and rhizoid cell developmental program in epidermal cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited overexpression and loss-of-function studies.

claims.claim: The RSL class I mechanism is likely to be ancient and have originated in the common ancestor of all land plants.
claims.source: This suggests that the RSL class I mechanism is likely to be ancient and have originated in the common ancestor of all land plants.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the conservation of RSL class I gene function across land plant lineages.

claims.claim: RSL class I genes from the moss P. patens, liverwort M. polymorpha or monocot rice restore root hair development in the roothairless A. thaliana mutants that lack RSL class I gene function.
claims.source: RSL class I genes from the moss P. patens, liverwort M. polymorpha or monocot rice restore root hair development in the roothairless A. thaliana mutants that lack RSL class I gene function (Menand et al., 2007; Proust et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on cross-species complementation experiments.

claims.claim: The molecular function of RSL class I proteins is conserved among moss, liverwort, rice, and Arabidopsis lineages.
claims.source: This indicates that the molecular function of RSL class I proteins is conserved among these lineages.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the complementation data cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Negative regulation of RSL class I genes in A. thaliana suppresses the formation of root hairs in a subset of root epidermal cells.
claims.source: Negative regulation of RSL class I genes in A. thaliana suppresses the formation of root hairs in a subset of root epidermal cells (Lin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on negative regulation in Arabidopsis.

claims.claim: The A. thaliana root epidermis comprises two cell types; trichoblasts that go on to differentiate into root hair cells and atrichoblasts that differentiate as root hairless epidermal cells.
claims.source: The A. thaliana root epidermis comprises two cell types; trichoblasts that go on to differentiate into root hair cells and atrichoblasts that differentiate as root hairless epidermal cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Arabidopsis root epidermis development.

claims.claim: RSL class I genes, AtRHD6 and AtRSL1, are expressed early in development of trichoblasts before root hairs emerge and they positively regulate the expression of genes involved in root hair differentiation.
claims.source: RSL class I genes, AtRHD6 and AtRSL1, are expressed early in development of trichoblasts before root hairs emerge and they positively regulate the expression of genes involved in root hair differentiation (Menand et al., 2007; Yi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression and function.

claims.claim: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression is repressed in atrichoblasts by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2).
claims.source: AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 expression is repressed in atrichoblasts by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2) (Di Cristina et al., 1996; Bernhardt et al., 2005; Bernhardt et al., 2003; Koshino-Kimura et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on GL2 function.

claims.claim: AtGL2 proteins directly bind to L1 box motifs on the promoters of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 and inhibit root hair initiation by repressing the transcription of these positive regulators of root hair development.
claims.source: AtGL2 proteins directly bind to L1 box motifs on the promoters of AtRHD6 and AtRSL1 and inhibit root hair initiation by repressing the transcription of these positive regulators of root hair development (Lin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on GL2 binding and function.

claims.claim: GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes (liverworts, mosses and hornworts).
claims.source: Furthermore, GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes (liverworts, mosses and hornworts) (Zalewski et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on GL2 gene distribution.

claims.claim: Four mutants, ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10, develop no or very few rhizoid precursor cells and consequently develop few rhizoids.
claims.source: We identified four mutants, ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 that develop no or very few rhizoid precursor cells and consequently develop few rhizoids (Figure 1A–L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and microscopy images shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The few rhizoids phenotype segregated as a single locus in the F1 generation of ST45-2 and ST49-10 backcrosses to wild type.
claims.source: The few rhizoids phenotype segregated as a single locus in each F1 generation, that is 50% of plants developed few rhizoids and 50% were indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by segregation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The few rhizoids phenotype co-segregated with the hygromycin resistance marker gene on the T-DNA in both ST45-2 and ST49-10 segregating F1 populations.
claims.source: Furthermore, the few rhizoids phenotype co-segregated with the hygromycin resistance marker gene on the T-DNA in both ST45-2 and ST49-10 segregating F1 populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-segregation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There is a single T-DNA insertion that is tightly linked to the few rhizoids phenotype in ST45-2.
claims.source: Based on the ratios of hygromycin resistant to hygromycin sensitive F1 plants, there is a single T-DNA insertion that is tightly linked to the few rhizoids phenotype in ST45-2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the segregation ratios observed in the F1 generation.

claims.claim: There are two T-DNA insertions in ST49-10; one responsible for the few rhizoids phenotype and a second unlinked T-DNA insertion.
claims.source: There are two T-DNA insertions in ST49-10; one responsible for the few rhizoids phenotype and a second unlinked T-DNA insertion.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the segregation ratios observed in the F1 generation.

claims.claim: A T-DNA insertion was identified within a 1.2 kb region of the M. polymorpha genome in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10.
claims.source: We identified a T-DNA insertion within a 1.2 kb region of the M. polymorpha genome in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 (Figure 1M, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that this genomic region is involved in rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TAIL-PCR data and the T-DNA insertion map shown in Figure 1M.

claims.claim: No transcript overlapped with the T-DNA insertion sites in any of the four few rhizoids mutants based on mapping the M. polymorpha gametophyte transcriptome sequences onto the genome assembly.
claims.source: Mapping the M. polymorpha gametophyte transcriptome sequences onto the genome assembly (Honkanen et al., 2016) indicated that no transcript overlapped with the T-DNA insertion sites in any of the four few rhizoids mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of transcriptome data.

claims.claim: A transcript fragment that mapped next to the right border of the T-DNA insertions was expressed at higher levels in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 than in wild type.
claims.source: A transcript fragment that mapped next to the right border of the T-DNA insertions was expressed at higher levels in each of the few rhizoids mutants ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2 and ST49-10 than in wild type (Figure 1N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1N.

claims.claim: 3' and 5' RACE-PCR identified a 1.2 kb intron-less polyadenylated transcript named FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1).
claims.source: To identify the full-length transcript we performed 3' and 5' RACE-PCR. This identified a 1.2 kb intron-less polyadenylated transcript (Supplementary file 2) that we named FEW RHIZOIDS1 (MpFRH1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RACE-PCR experimental data.

claims.claim: In each of the four few rhizoids mutants a T-DNA is inserted 5' of a gene encoding a 1.2 kb transcript that is expressed at higher levels than in wild type.
claims.source: Together these data indicate that in each of the four few rhizoids mutants a T-DNA is inserted 5' of a gene encoding a 1.2 kb transcript that is expressed at higher levels than in wild type.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the T-DNA insertion mapping and expression data.

claims.claim: The majority of plants transformed with MpFRH1 under the control of the strong constitutive rice ACTIN1 promoter (88 out of 103) developed very few or no rhizoids.
claims.source: The majority of the resulting transformed plants (88 out of 103) developed very few or no rhizoids (Figure 2C,G,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments and images in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Steady state levels of MpFRH1 transcript were higher than wild type in each of the transformed lines with few rhizoids, while wild type levels of MpFRH1 transcript were observed in the lines with wild type phenotype.
claims.source: Steady state levels of MpFRH1 transcript were higher than wild type in each of the transformed lines with few rhizoids, while wild type levels of MpFRH1 transcript were observed in the lines with wild type phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Over-expression of the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype of the ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 T-DNA insertion mutants.
claims.source: This indicates that over-expression of the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype of the ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 T-DNA insertion mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overexpression and phenotype data.

claims.claim: Each of ST21-1, ST49-10, ST45-2 and ST33-2 is a gain-of-function mutant, in which elevated expression of MpFRH1 results in reduced number of rhizoid precursor cells and rhizoids.
claims.source: This suggests that each is a gain-of-function mutant, in which elevated expression of MpFRH1 results in reduced number of rhizoid precursor cells and rhizoids.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overexpression and mutant phenotype data.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
claims.source: Together these findings indicate that MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the gain-of-function mutant and overexpression data.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines lacked multicellular mucilage papillae that develop in the epidermis near meristematic regions of wild type plants.
claims.source: Furthermore, like Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants, MpFRH1GOF mutants and proACT:MpFRH1 lines lacked multicellular mucilage papillae that develop in the epidermis near meristematic regions of wild type plants (Figure 2Q–T).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2Q-T.

claims.claim: Gemmae only rarely develop in Mprsl1, MpFRH1GOF, proACT:MpFRH1 lines and the gemma cups were generally empty.
claims.source: By contrast, gemmae only rarely develop in Mprsl1, MpFRH1GOF, proACT:MpFRH1 lines and the gemma cups were generally empty (Figure 2N–P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2N-P.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 negatively regulates the development of the same structures – rhizoids, gemmae and epidermal papillae – that are positively regulated by MpRSL1.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that MpFRH1 negatively regulates the development of the same structures – rhizoids, gemmae and epidermal papillae – that are positively regulated by MpRSL1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the phenotypic similarities between MpFRH1 gain-of-function and Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants.

claims.claim: There are no long open reading frames in the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript sequence and the sequence is not similar to any Arabidopsis protein coding sequences.
claims.source: There are no long open reading frames in the 1.2 kb MpFRH1 transcript sequence and the sequence is not similar to any Arabidopsis protein coding sequences.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic sequence analysis.

claims.claim: The 21 nt predicted miRNA mpo-MIR11861 (UGUGUGAGAAGAGGCCAAUGU) maps to the same genomic location as the MpFRH1 transcript.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the 21 nt predicted miRNA mpo-MIR11861 (UGUGUGAGAAGAGGCCAAUGU) maps to the same genomic location as the MpFRH1 transcript (Tsuzuki et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior miRNA prediction work and genomic mapping.

claims.claim: Over-expression of a 150 bp fragment of the MpFRH1 transcript containing the predicted miRNA hairpin structure in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype.
claims.source: Over-expression of the 150 bp miRNA hairpin-containing fragment (MpFRH1miRNA) in the wild type background was sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype (Figure 4C,I,O, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that MpFRH1 is a miRNA gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The presence of the mature MpFRH1 miRNA was verified using stem-loop PCR.
claims.source: The presence of the mature MpFRH1 miRNA was verified using stem-loop PCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by stem-loop PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Elevated levels of the MpFRH1 pri-miRNA transcript in MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants give rise to elevated levels of mature MpFRH1 miRNA.
claims.source: In the stem-loop PCR a 60 bp band corresponding to the MpFRH1 miRNA and a fused stem-loop sequence was stronger in the MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutant samples compared to wild type, suggesting that elevated levels of the MpFRH1 pri-miRNA transcript in these mutants give rise to elevated levels of mature MpFRH1 miRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the stem-loop PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Transformed plants over-expressing proACT:MpFRH1noATG (with mutated start codons) developed very few rhizoids similar to the four MpFRH1GOF lines and proACT:MpFRH1 lines.
claims.source: Transformed plants over-expressing proACT:MpFRH1noATG developed very few rhizoids similar to the four MpFRH1GOF lines and proACT:MpFRH1 lines (Figure 4D,J,P, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Transformed plants overexpressing either MpFRH1PSORF1 or MpFRH1PSORF2 did not have defects in rhizoid development and were undistinguishable from wild type plants.
claims.source: Transformed plants overexpressing either MpFRH1PSORF1 or MpFRH1PSORF2 did not have defects in rhizoid development and were undistinguishable from wild type plants (Figure 4E–F,K–L,Q–R, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA that represses rhizoid development.
claims.source: Together, these findings indicate that MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA that represses rhizoid development.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the overexpression experiments with different MpFRH1 constructs.

claims.claim: One of the predicted MpFRH1 miRNA targets was a 21 bp sequence on the MpRSL1 mRNA.
claims.source: One of the predicted targets was a 21 bp sequence on the MpRSL1 mRNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic target prediction using TargetFinder.

claims.claim: The steady state levels of MpRSL1 mRNA were lower in all four MpFRH1GOF mutants and the four proACT1:MpFRH1 lines tested.
claims.source: The steady state levels of MpRSL1 mRNA were lower in all four MpFRH1GOF mutants and the four proACT1:MpFRH1 lines tested (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The amplified MpRSL1 mRNA fragment from 5'RLM-RACE PCR assay terminated within the predicted MpFRH1 target site, indicating MpFRH1 miRNA mediates cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
claims.source: The amplified MpRSL1 mRNA fragment terminated within the predicted MpFRH1 target site (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 3), indicating MpFRH1 miRNA mediates cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 5'RLM-RACE PCR data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: The steady state levels of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs were similar in wild type and MpFRH1 gain of function mutants suggesting that they are not MpFRH1 miRNA targets.
claims.source: The steady state levels of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs were similar in wild type and MpFRH1 gain of function mutants suggesting that they are not MpFRH1 miRNA targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The predicted MpFRH1 miRNA target site on the orthologs of each of the three other predicted target mRNAs is not conserved among liverworts.
claims.source: Furthermore, the predicted MpFRH1 miRNA target site on the orthologs of each of these three mRNAs is not conserved among liverworts (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates rhizoid development by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
claims.source: We conclude that MpFRH1 miRNA negatively regulates rhizoid development by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RLM-RACE and expression data.

claims.claim: Twenty-five out of the 26 transformants of MpFRH1GOF2 mutants transformed with the wild type version of MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt) were rhizoidless like MpFRH1GOF2 plants, while only one transformant developed rhizoids.
claims.source: Twenty-five out of the 26 transformants were rhizoidless like MpFRH1GOF2 plants, while only one transformant developed rhizoids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Expression of the wild type version of MpRSL1 from the MpEF1∝ promoter does not suppress the rhizoidless phenotype of MpFRH1GOF2.
claims.source: This indicates that expression of the wild type version of MpRSL1 from the MpEF1∝ promoter does not suppress the rhizoidless phenotype of MpFRH1GOF2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the transformation data.

claims.claim: Seven out of ten lines transformed with the MpFRH1 miRNA resistant version of MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res) developed abundant rhizoids on the ventral thallus surface and two lines developed rhizoids on both ventral and dorsal surfaces of the thallus, while a single line was rhizoidless.
claims.source: Seven of these transformed lines developed abundant rhizoids on the ventral thallus surface and two lines developed rhizoids on both ventral and dorsal surfaces of the thallus, while a single line was rhizoidless and was phenotypically identical to MpFRH1GOF2 plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: None (0%) of the gemmalings expressing the wild type MpRSL1 in the MpFRH1GOF2 background (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids.
claims.source: None (0%) of the gemmalings expressing the wild type MpRSL1 in the MpFRH1GOF2 background (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Most (88.9%) gemmalings transformed with the miRNA resistant form of the MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids.
claims.source: In contrast, most (88.9%) gemmalings transformed with the miRNA resistant form of the MpRSL1 (proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res MpFRH1GOF2) developed rhizoids (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Gemmae developed in the gemma cups of MpFRH1GOF2 plants transformed with proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res, while the gemma cups of proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2 plants were mostly empty.
claims.source: Gemmae developed in the gemma cups of MpFRH1GOF2 plants transformed with proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res, while similar to the MpFRH1GOF2 plants the gemma cups of proMpEF1α:MpRSL1wt MpFRH1GOF2 plants were mostly empty (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The restoration of gemma development by the proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res construct in the MpFRH1GOF2 background demonstrates that MpRSL1 is a target of MpFRH1 regulation during gemma development.
claims.source: The restoration of gemma development by the proMpEF1α:MpRSL1res construct in the MpFRH1GOF2 background demonstrates that MpRSL1 is a target of MpFRH1 regulation during gemma development.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment data.

claims.claim: MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1 by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA during the development of structures derived from single epidermal cells in M. polymorpha.
claims.source: Together these data are consistent with the hypothesis that MpFRH1 negatively regulates MpRSL1 by mediating the cleavage of the MpRSL1 mRNA during the development of structures derived from single epidermal cells in M. polymorpha.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claims.claim: Steady state MpFRH1 transcript levels were lower than wild type in the Mprsl1-1 and Mprsl1-2 loss-of-function mutant alleles, but higher than wild type in the MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutant alleles MpRSLGOF1-3.
claims.source: Steady state MpFRH1 transcript levels were lower than wild type in the Mprsl1-1 and Mprsl1-2 loss-of-function mutant alleles, but higher than wild type in the MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutant alleles MpRSLGOF1-3 (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: MpRSL1 positively regulates steady state MpFRH1 transcript level.
claims.source: These results indicate that MpRSL1 positively regulates steady state MpFRH1 transcript level.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the expression data in MpRSL1 mutants.

claims.claim: Functional MpRSL1 is not required for baseline MpFRH1 expression; a low level of MpFRH1 mRNA persists in the Mprsl1 complete loss-of-function mutant background.
claims.source: However, functional MpRSL1 is not required for baseline MpFRH1 expression; a low level of MpFRH1 mRNA persists in the Mprsl1 complete loss-of-function mutant background (Figure 6), suggesting that other mechanisms also contribute to the regulation of MpFRH1 expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The positive regulation of MpFRH1 expression by MpRSL1, which is in turn targeted by MpFRH1 miRNA, indicates that MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 miRNA form a regulatory loop with negative feedback.
claims.source: The positive regulation of MpFRH1 expression by MpRSL1, which is in turn targeted by MpFRH1 miRNA, indicates that MpRSL1 and MpFRH1 miRNA form a regulatory loop with negative feedback.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mutual regulation data.

claims.claim: YFP fluorescence, indicative of MpFRH1 promoter activity, was observed in the rhizoid precursor cells of proMpFRH1:3xYFP:NLS transformed plants.
claims.source: We observed YFP fluorescence, indicative of MpFRH1 promoter activity, in the rhizoid precursor cells, which on young gemmae can be distinguished from non-rhizoid precursor cells based on their strongly reduced chlorophyll autofluorescence (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

results.result: A forward genetic screen in M. polymorpha identified four T-DNA insertion mutants (ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2, ST49-10) with few rhizoids. Genetic and molecular analysis revealed that all four mutants have T-DNA insertions within a 1.2 kb genomic region upstream of a transcript named MpFRH1, and these insertions result in elevated MpFRH1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C33 provide converging genetic (segregation analysis, co-segregation with marker), molecular (TAIL-PCR, transcriptome mapping, qRT-PCR), and phenotypic evidence that T-DNA insertions upstream of MpFRH1 cause elevated expression and the few rhizoids phenotype. The data are internally consistent and well-documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: Overexpression of MpFRH1 under a constitutive promoter in wild-type M. polymorpha is sufficient to reproduce the few rhizoids phenotype, demonstrating that MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and that the original mutants are gain-of-function alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 demonstrate that elevated MpFRH1 expression is sufficient to cause the few rhizoids phenotype through transformation experiments with appropriate controls. The correlation between MpFRH1 transcript levels and phenotype severity (C35) strengthens the causal relationship. This establishes MpFRH1 as a negative regulator.

results.result: MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants and overexpression lines phenocopy Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants, lacking not only rhizoids but also mucilage papillae and gemmae, suggesting that MpFRH1 negatively regulates the same developmental structures positively regulated by MpRSL1.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 document phenotypic similarities between MpFRH1 gain-of-function and Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants across multiple structures (rhizoids, papillae, gemmae), supported by microscopy data in Figure 2. This phenotypic convergence provides strong evidence for MpFRH1 acting as a negative regulator of MpRSL1-dependent developmental programs.

results.result: MpFRH1 encodes a functional miRNA rather than a protein. The 1.2 kb transcript lacks long ORFs, contains a predicted miRNA hairpin structure, and overexpression of either the full transcript, a 150 bp miRNA-containing fragment, or a version with mutated start codons all produce the few rhizoids phenotype, while overexpression of putative small ORFs does not. Stem-loop PCR confirms the presence of mature miRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 provide multiple lines of evidence that MpFRH1 functions as a miRNA: sequence analysis (C42), prior prediction (C43), functional complementation with minimal miRNA-containing fragment (C44), detection of mature miRNA (C45-C46), and negative results with ORF-only constructs (C48). The experimental design systematically rules out protein-coding function.

results.result: MpFRH1 miRNA directly targets MpRSL1 mRNA for cleavage. Bioinformatic prediction identified a target site on MpRSL1 mRNA, MpRSL1 transcript levels are reduced in MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants, and 5'RLM-RACE PCR demonstrates cleavage within the predicted target site. Other predicted targets show no evidence of regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C55 establish MpRSL1 as the bona fide target through computational prediction (C50), expression analysis (C51), and direct demonstration of cleavage at the predicted site (C52). The negative results for other predicted targets (C53-C54) strengthen the specificity of the MpFRH1-MpRSL1 interaction. The 5'RLM-RACE data provide direct molecular evidence of miRNA-mediated cleavage.

results.result: Expression of an MpFRH1 miRNA-resistant version of MpRSL1 (MpRSL1res) rescues the rhizoidless and gemma-deficient phenotypes of MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants, while wild-type MpRSL1 does not, confirming that MpRSL1 is the functionally relevant target of MpFRH1 miRNA during development of structures derived from single epidermal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 provide the critical genetic rescue experiment demonstrating that MpRSL1 is the functionally relevant target. The contrast between wild-type MpRSL1 (no rescue, C56-C57, C59) and miRNA-resistant MpRSL1 (rescue, C58, C60-C61) is striking and well-quantified. This establishes causality and functional relevance of the miRNA-target interaction in vivo.

results.result: MpRSL1 positively regulates MpFRH1 expression, creating a negative feedback loop. MpFRH1 transcript levels are reduced in Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants and elevated in MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutants, though baseline MpFRH1 expression persists in the absence of functional MpRSL1.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 demonstrate reciprocal regulation through qRT-PCR analysis in multiple MpRSL1 mutant backgrounds (Figure 6). The correlation between MpRSL1 activity and MpFRH1 levels is clear, though the persistence of baseline MpFRH1 expression (C66) appropriately indicates additional regulatory inputs. This establishes a feedback regulatory circuit.

results.result: MpFRH1 promoter activity is detected in rhizoid precursor cells, elongating rhizoids, and mucilage papillae, as shown by promoter-reporter analysis. The signal in rhizoid precursor cells is stronger than in surrounding cells and appears transiently in mucilage papillae.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 document MpFRH1 expression patterns using promoter-reporter constructs with appropriate controls (MpIRE promoter, C70). The confocal microscopy data (Figure 7) clearly show cell-type-specific expression. The inference about differential promoter activity (C71) is well-supported by the control comparison, and the observation of variable signal in papillae (C73) is appropriately interpreted as transient expression.

results.result: The FRH1 miRNA target site is 100% conserved across twelve liverwort species representing two major liverwort clades but is absent from RSL class I transcripts in moss, lycophyte, and angiosperm lineages, indicating that FRH1-mediated regulation evolved early in the liverwort lineage while different negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in other land plant lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C77-C78 present comparative sequence analysis across land plant lineages (Figure 8). The 100% conservation within liverworts and complete absence outside liverworts provides strong evidence for lineage-specific evolution of this regulatory mechanism. The sequence alignments are clearly presented and the evolutionary inference is well-justified.

results.result: The M. polymorpha RSL1 promoter lacks L1-box sequences that mediate GL2-dependent repression in Arabidopsis, and there is no evidence for class IV homeodomain protein involvement in MpRSL1 regulation, indicating that the miRNA-based mechanism is distinct from the Arabidopsis regulatory system.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 provide negative evidence through sequence analysis showing absence of L1-box motifs. Combined with the positive evidence for miRNA-mediated regulation, this supports the conclusion that M. polymorpha uses a different regulatory mechanism than Arabidopsis. The inference is appropriately cautious given the negative nature of the evidence.

results.result: The discovery of liverwort-specific miRNA regulation of RSL class I genes, combined with the known GL2-mediated regulation in Arabidopsis and the absence of FRH1 target sites in Arabidopsis RSL genes, demonstrates that at least two independent negative regulatory mechanisms have evolved to control the conserved RSL class I transcription factors in different land plant lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 synthesize the comparative data to reach the major evolutionary conclusion. The evidence for independent evolution is strong: (1) different molecular mechanisms (miRNA vs. transcriptional repressor), (2) absence of FRH1 in Arabidopsis (C83), (3) absence of FRH1 target sites in Arabidopsis RSL genes (C83), and (4) lineage-specific distribution of each mechanism. This is the central evolutionary finding of the paper.

results.result: Different modes of negative regulation for RSL class I genes likely evolved more than twice during land plant evolution, as the mechanisms in moss and grasses remain unknown, FRH1 is absent from these lineages, and GL2 is not conserved in bryophytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 extend the evolutionary argument to other lineages based on absence of known regulators. While the negative evidence (absence of FRH1 and GL2 in various lineages) is documented, the positive claim that different mechanisms exist in these lineages (C86, C91) is speculative. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('likely', 'remain to be discovered'), but the claim goes beyond what is directly demonstrated.

results.result: MpFRH1 miRNA is found only in liverworts and has been conserved for over 405 million years since the divergence of major liverwort clades, possibly existing since the divergence of liverworts from other land plants approximately 440 million years ago, indicating that FRH1-mediated regulation has been extant since the period of land plant morphological diversification.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 combine sequence conservation data (C92-C93) with phylogenetic dating from cited literature to establish the evolutionary age of the FRH1 mechanism. The conservation data are solid (C75, C92-C93), and the phylogenetic dates are appropriately cited (C93-C94). The inference about timing relative to land plant diversification (C95) is reasonable given the dates, though somewhat speculative about functional significance.

results.result: The authors speculate that the evolution of novel negative regulatory mechanisms like FRH1 may have been associated with gene regulatory network rewiring during morphological diversification, that MpFRH1 may function non-cell-autonomously in spatial patterning, and that evolution of lineage-specific negative regulation may have contributed to the radiation of land plant morphological diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C105 present speculative hypotheses about evolutionary mechanisms and potential functions. While these are interesting ideas that follow logically from the data, they are explicitly speculative (using 'may', 'possible', 'if correct') and lack direct experimental support. These represent future research directions rather than established results.

results.result: RSL class I genes are ancient, conserved transcription factors that function as molecular switches necessary and sufficient to induce root hair and rhizoid development across land plants, with conserved molecular function demonstrated by cross-species complementation experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C16 summarize established knowledge from prior work (all supported by citations) that provides essential context for the current study. These claims about RSL class I gene function and conservation are well-established in the field and appropriately cited. This background is necessary to frame the significance of discovering lineage-specific negative regulation.

results.result: In Arabidopsis thaliana, RSL class I genes (AtRHD6 and AtRSL1) are negatively regulated by the homeodomain protein GLABRA2 (GL2), which directly binds L1-box motifs on their promoters to repress transcription in atrichoblasts. GL2 genes have not been identified in bryophytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C21, C23, C82 summarize prior work on Arabidopsis root hair regulation (all cited) that establishes the contrasting regulatory mechanism. This background is essential for the comparative evolutionary analysis and is well-documented in the literature. The absence of GL2 in bryophytes (C23) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Streptophyte algal ancestors of land plants had little cell-type diversity and did not develop distinct organs, but many transcription factor families previously thought to have evolved in land plants were already present in streptophyte algae.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 cite prior research on algal morphology and transcription factor evolution to provide evolutionary context. These are appropriately cited background claims that frame the discussion about how morphological complexity evolved in land plants.

results.result: A forward genetic screen in Marchantia polymorpha identified four T-DNA insertion mutants (ST21-1, ST33-2, ST45-2, ST49-10) with few rhizoids. These mutants have T-DNA insertions in a 1.2 kb genomic region that does not overlap with annotated transcripts but is adjacent to an upregulated transcript fragment, identified by RACE-PCR as MpFRH1.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers acknowledge the quality of the genetic screen and characterization of the mutants. Reviewer 1 states 'the quality of data is generally very high' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the strategy taken in this study is straightforward and the quality of the evidence and presentation are high.' No concerns were raised about the mutant identification or initial characterization.

results.result: Overexpression of the full-length MpFRH1 transcript under a constitutive promoter reproduced the few rhizoids phenotype in wild-type plants, demonstrating that MpFRH1 is a negative regulator of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation and that the original mutants are gain-of-function alleles.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this conclusion without objection. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'clearly showed the mechanism of negative regulation in Marchantia polymorpha' and Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'clearly show that MpFRH1 targets MpRSL1 transcripts for down-regulation to inhibit rhizoid development.'

results.result: MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants and overexpression lines also lack mucilage papillae and gemmae, phenocopying Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants, suggesting MpFRH1 negatively regulates the same developmental structures positively regulated by MpRSL1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these pleiotropic phenotypes. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'MpFRH1 also regulates development of apical papillae and gemmae, suggesting its role on various types of epidermal cell differentiation,' accepting this broader regulatory role.

results.result: MpFRH1 encodes a miRNA rather than a protein. The transcript lacks long ORFs, contains a predicted miRNA hairpin structure, and overexpression of just the hairpin region or constructs with mutated start codons reproduces the phenotype, while overexpression of constructs designed to express only putative small ORFs does not affect rhizoid development. Stem-loop PCR confirmed the presence of mature miRNA.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern about the sufficiency of the evidence: 'To prove that MpFRH1 encodes miRNA, I think stem-loop PCR is not sufficient. Northern blot analysis is a more direct and reliable approach to detect miRNA of MpFRH1. If possible, I suggest to include these data to strengthen this point.' This indicates the reviewer finds the miRNA identification uncertain without additional validation.

results.result: MpFRH1 miRNA targets MpRSL1 mRNA for cleavage. Bioinformatic prediction identified MpRSL1 as a target, MpRSL1 mRNA levels are reduced in MpFRH1 gain-of-function lines, and 5'RLM-RACE PCR showed cleavage at the predicted target site. Other predicted targets showed no expression changes and lack conserved target sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern: 'The main text states that the MpRSL1 mRNA fragment terminated at the putative cleavage site, although Figure 3B only shows the gene structure and the predicted site. The authors should provide such experimental data, or revise the main text and Materials and methods.' This indicates the cleavage data presentation is insufficient or unclear, making the targeting mechanism uncertain.

results.result: Expression of a miRNA-resistant version of MpRSL1 (with mutations in the target site) rescues the rhizoidless phenotype of MpFRH1 gain-of-function mutants, while wild-type MpRSL1 does not, confirming that MpRSL1 is the functionally relevant target of MpFRH1 miRNA during rhizoid and gemma development.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this genetic rescue experiment without objection. Reviewer 2 notes 'Using multiple mutant versions of MpFRH1, the authors clearly show that MpFRH1 targets MpRSL1 transcripts for down-regulation,' implicitly accepting the rescue data as part of the clear demonstration.

results.result: MpRSL1 positively regulates MpFRH1 expression, forming a negative feedback loop. MpFRH1 transcript levels are lower in Mprsl1 loss-of-function mutants and higher in MpRSL1 gain-of-function mutants, though baseline MpFRH1 expression persists in complete loss-of-function backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 requests clarification: 'The subsection "MpRSL1 positively regulates MpFRH1 transcript level" starts without any explanation to study the hypothesis. I recommend to mention the motivation for why authors want to test if MpRSL1 regulates MpFRH1 expression.' This suggests the reviewer finds the rationale and interpretation of this feedback loop unclear or insufficiently motivated.

results.result: MpFRH1 promoter activity is detected in rhizoid precursor cells, elongating rhizoids, and mucilage papillae, with stronger expression in rhizoid precursor cells than surrounding cells. The expression appears transient in mucilage papillae.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises an important question about the spatio-temporal dynamics: 'This raises the question how MpRSL1 is activated to specify gemma epidermal cells as the rhizoid precursor cells, in which MpFRH1 are also expressed... More information about spatio-temporal pattern of the MpFRH1 promoter activity during gemma development would be helpful for better understanding of the molecular mechanism of rhizoid precursor cell differentiation.' This indicates uncertainty about how the antagonistic relationship between MpFRH1 and MpRSL1 is resolved spatially and temporally.

results.result: The FRH1 miRNA target site is 100% conserved across twelve liverwort species but absent in RSL class I transcripts of moss, lycophyte, and angiosperm species, indicating that FRH1-mediated regulation evolved specifically in the liverwort lineage.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this evolutionary conclusion. Reviewer 1 notes 'It is also interesting that this negative regulation of RSL class I gene is conserved only in liverwort, suggesting that different from RSL class I gene, "independent negative regulatory mechanisms evolved in different lineages during land plant evolution" as the authors pointed out.'

results.result: Different negative regulatory mechanisms evolved independently in liverworts (MpFRH1 miRNA) and angiosperms (GL2 transcription factor).
